scope_note: Built from the reviewed backend articles: pet-plastic-bottles. General handling advice, not proof that a local facility accepts the item.
steps: Empty out every last drop so it doesn't contaminate paper or other plastics.
If it held a sweet drink or milk, give it a quick rinse with a little water and let it drain.
Leave the cap on or take it off, whichever your waste bank or local collector asks for.
Flatten the bottle if you need to save space before taking it to a waste bank or recycling drop-off.
caution: Don't keep refilling single-use PET bottles for food or hot drinks. Whether caps and labels are accepted depends on your local recycler's rules.

scope_note: Built from the reviewed backend articles: used-household-batteries. General handling advice, not proof that a local facility accepts the item.
steps: Store used batteries somewhere cool and dry, away from children and metal objects.
Cover both terminals of lithium or coin batteries with non-conductive electrical tape, or put each one in its own bag, so they can't short-circuit.

caution: Never take apart, puncture, crush, or burn used batteries. If a battery is swollen, leaking, or physically damaged, contact a licensed hazardous waste handler or the manufacturer for special handling.

evidence.text: Used batteries can still hold energy, and some contain hazardous materials. Lithium, coin, and rechargeable batteries need a specialist collection point, not the trash or mixed recycling. Check the battery type and what the collector accepts.

scope_note: Built from the reviewed backend articles: food-scraps-and-composting, preventing-household-food-waste. General handling advice, not proof that a local facility accepts the item.
steps: Keep vegetable scraps, fruit peels, coffee grounds, and dry leaves separate from plastic and packaging.
Cut large pieces into smaller ones so they break down faster.

Mix at least two to three parts dry (brown) material by volume, such as dry leaves or shredded cardboard without coating, tape, or glue, for every one part wet (green) material. Use a composter that lets air in, not an airtight container.
Turn it regularly and keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Let the compost mature before you use it; material that's only been dried isn't compost yet.
caution: Leave out meat, fish, bones, dairy, oil, pet waste, painted wood, and diseased plants. Home composters usually don't reach industrial processing conditions, so packaging labeled compostable isn't automatically suitable. Normal looks and smell don't prove food is safe. Don't taste it to check. If you don't know how long or how warm it was stored, or it wasn't stored safely, don't eat it.

evidence.text: Fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, eggshells, and dry leaves can be composted at home or sent to a community organics program, so they don't produce methane in a landfill.
